# Hitopadesha

-> 140 <-

The war having now arrived, the <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>ruddy goose, here serving as a minister</gloss> says: "Your Majesty, war is not the proper course at the very beginning. For: What kind of servant is he, or what kind of minister, who at the very outset advises the King to prepare for battle and abandon his own territory without deliberation? Furthermore: One should strive to conquer enemies by means other than war, for victory between two combatants is seen to be uncertain. Moreover: One should strive to manage the enemy through <term>sama</term> <gloss>conciliation</gloss>, <term>dana</term> <gloss>gifts</gloss>, <term>bheda</term> <gloss>sowing dissension</gloss>, either collectively or separately, but never through war. Additionally: Every man is a hero so long as he has not encountered a battle; who would not be full of pride before seeing the strength of the opponent? Besides: A heavy stone is not moved by living beings as effectively as it is by mechanical means; achieving great success through small efforts is the great fruit of wise counsel. But seeing that war is now upon us, let us act accordingly." For:

<note>The following section provides a Bengali translation of the Sanskrit verses above.</note>

The war having arrived, the <term>Chakravaka</term> says: "O Great King, at the beginning war is not the duty. For what kind of servant is he, and what kind of minister is he, who beforehand advises the King to prepare for battle and to leave his own place without considering the matter? Furthermore, one should make efforts to conquer the opponent through conciliation and other means; one should never do it through battle, because among two people fighting, it is not known for certain whose victory it will be. Furthermore, one should strive to settle the opponent through conciliation, gifts, or dissension, either individually or through all of them; one should never do it through war. Furthermore, all people are brave when no war has been fought, because..."

<summary>The minister Chakravaka advises the King against immediate war, emphasizing that diplomacy, bribery, and sowing discord are superior to the uncertainty of physical combat. He argues that true statesmanship achieves great results through minimal force and careful deliberation.</summary>
